name: Process: lifecycle, Agile, Scrum, backlog, Definition of Done
shape_md: None of the nine samples is about the lifecycle, Agile or Scrum, but sessions 1, 2 and 4 are on the paper. Expect the same shapes with a team, a backlog or a Sprint in the story.
one_md: Name the situation in the course's words and give the rule the slides give for it, not the quick or senior option.
spot_md:
- A short story of a team going wrong (nobody agreed an order, a push broke everyone, it only runs on one laptop) is asked like Q5: name the failure. Session 1 pairs each failure with its answer.
- A change in a project (a library swap, a hard-coded shortcut, a crash on an empty list) is asked like Q2: which kind of change is it? Same behaviour and unchanged tests means refactoring.
- A Scrum scenario (a request from outside mid-Sprint, a red CI check the day before the Review, a Retrospective that turns into blame) is asked like Q4: what follows? The answer states the rule.
- A pasted backlog or Definition of Done is asked like Q7: name two problems, say how you would change it, say which problem each change solves. One or two sentences per part.
- "Which approach fits?" (Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban, XP) is asked like Q1: match the situation and cross out the rest.

basics.heading: Lifecycle, failures, Waterfall and Agile
basics.body_md:
The lifecycle has seven phases: Idea, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance. Development comes late and Maintenance never ends. After launch the cycle restarts at Design for one of four kinds of change: a bug (unintended behaviour), a feature (new behaviour), a refactor (same behaviour, new structure) or tech debt (a known, deliberate shortcut).

| A failure from slide 6 | What slide 8 answers |
|---|---|
| no shared plan, four people build four corners | Agile, Scrum |
| nobody can read it; change one thing, three others break | clean code, testing, TDD |
| a teammate's change breaks the build | version control, code reviews, CI |
| works on my machine | containerisation, automatic deployment |

Waterfall is linear: each phase is finished before the next, and the gate is an approved document. It suits fixed scope and fixed price. For software, requirements change (normal, not a failed analysis), feedback comes late and integration risk piles up. Agile runs the same phases in every short cycle, on a small slice.

basics.heading: Scrum on one page
basics.body_md:
The Product Owner owns and orders the backlog, and is one person. The Scrum Master makes the process work and removes impediments, and is not a manager. Developers build the Increment and decide how.

| Artifact | Its commitment |
|---|---|
| Product Backlog | Product Goal |
| Sprint Backlog | Sprint Goal |
| Increment | Definition of Done |

For a two-week Sprint: Refinement about 4 h, Planning 1 h, Daily 15 min, Review 1 h, Retrospective 1 h. The Daily is not a status report. The Review gathers feedback that changes the backlog. The Retrospective asks how the team worked, without blame.

A backlog item is an outcome a user gets, ordered by value and detailed only near the top. A Definition of Done line must be checkable, and "done except for tests" is not done. In this course it is a green CI check.

checks.q_md: Which Scrum artifact commits to the Definition of Done?
checks.why_md: Product Backlog to Product Goal, Sprint Backlog to Sprint Goal, Increment to Definition of Done.

checks.q_md: How long is the Daily in a two-week Sprint?
checks.why_md: Fifteen minutes. The 4 hours belong to Refinement and the hour to Planning, Review and Retrospective.

method: Name the situation in the course's words: a failure from slide 6, a kind of change, a ceremony, a role, a backlog item.
Recall the rule the slides give for it. The stem usually quotes the situation from the slide.
Cross out options that decide by speed, seniority or size: "quick win first", "the director asked", "three tests pass".
Pick the option that states the rule, and give the reason in one sentence.
Open, with a pasted backlog or Definition of Done: two problems (a task, a standard, a wish), the rewrite, which problem each change solves.

worked.title: A Definition of Done question, same shape as Q4
worked.question_md:
Two days before the Sprint Review, the flashcard-trainer group has the Leitner-box item in the Done column. Their Definition of Done says: "The CI check is green. The README says how to use the new behaviour." CI is green, but the README still has the old text. Ana says: "The code works, so it is done." What follows from the Definition of Done?

- a) The item is done: the code works, and the README is a detail for later
- b) The item is not done and does not ship until the README line is met
- c) The item is done, and the README goes into the next Sprint
- d) The item is 80% done, so the Review shows it with that label
steps_md: The Definition of Done is one bar for every item. Its lines are checks: green CI, README updated.
One line is not met, so the item misses the bar.
a, c and d all invent a middle state. The slide has none: "done except for" is not admissible.
worked.answer_md: **b.** The README line of the Definition of Done is not met, so the item is not done. An item that misses the Definition of Done does not ship, whatever the code does.

twists.twist_md: Q4 shape. On day 6 of a Sprint, a director outside the team asks two developers for a PDF export "for Friday".
twists.how_md: It goes to the Product Owner, who orders the backlog. Nobody outside decides how much goes into a Sprint.

twists.twist_md: Q1 shape. Two people maintain a tool and get small, varied requests every day; fixed two-week sprints keep breaking.
twists.how_md: Kanban: a board, a limit on work in progress, pull the next item when there is capacity. Scrum suits feature work, XP is about how code is written.

twists.twist_md: Q7 shape. A backlog line says "Tests", another says "Make it good", another "Do the database part".
twists.how_md: "Tests" is a standard for every item, so it belongs in the Definition of Done. "Make it good" cannot be checked. "Do the database part" is a task: nobody can tell when it is done.

twists.twist_md: Q4 shape. The Retrospective spends forty minutes on who broke CI and ends with an apology.
twists.how_md: That is blame, and nothing changes. A Retrospective covers how the team worked and what to change next Sprint, and ends with a concrete rule.

twists.twist_md: Q5 shape. A client sees the first version after nine months and wants something different. The manager says the analysis failed.
twists.how_md: Changing requirements are normal, not a failed analysis. The answer is working software sooner and frequent user involvement.

traps: "Three of four tests pass, so it is nearly done." There is no mostly done. An item that misses the Definition of Done is not done and does not ship.
"Quick wins first build momentum." The backlog is ordered by value, not by what is easiest to start.
"The Scrum Master assigns the tasks." The Scrum Master is not a manager. The Developers decide who does what, and the Product Owner decides the order.
"We value working software over documentation, so skip the README." The right side still has value. Working software is ranked above it, not instead of it.
say_md:
- Name the failure, then the course's answer: no shared plan, Agile and Scrum; nobody can read it, clean code and TDD; a change breaks the build, version control, review and CI; works on my machine, containers and deployment.
- A refactoring changes the structure and keeps the behaviour. A bug fix, a feature and tech debt do not.
- An item that misses the Definition of Done is not done and does not ship.
- The Product Owner orders the backlog by value. Nobody outside decides what goes into a Sprint.
- Review: feedback that changes the backlog. Retrospective: how the team worked, without blame.

scrum-q39.1: Line 2, "Do the database part", is a task, not an outcome: nobody can tell when it is done. Line 3, "Write tests for pricing", is a standard every item must meet, so it belongs in the Definition of Done.
scrum-q39.2: Line 4: "As a driver, I can see the price when I leave, so that I pay the right amount." Line 2: "As an attendant, I can reopen the program and see today's tickets, so that no car is lost overnight."
scrum-q39.3: Issuing a ticket goes first because it is the parking lot's core value: the backlog is ordered by value, not ease. Only the top three need detail because the lower items will change before they are built.
